nameStory: The name 'bifid hemp-nettle' comes from its split-lipped flowers - 'bifid' means divided into two parts. Despite its name, this plant isn't related to true hemp or stinging nettles, though its leaves do have a somewhat similar appearance to nettles. The 'weasel-like' genus name Galeopsis refers to the sneaky, pointed shape of the flower's face.
description: Bifid hemp-nettle is a European immigrant that's made itself at home in New England's disturbed soils. This annual herb grows 1-3 feet tall with a square stem typical of the mint family. Its most distinctive feature is the large, showy flowers with split lower lips that bloom in summer, usually in shades of pink, purple, or white. The plant has a somewhat weedy appearance with opposite, toothed leaves and a branching growth habit.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, two-lipped flowers with a distinctly split lower lip creating a 'bifid' or forked appearance. The upper lip forms a hood over the flower's center, and colors range from pink to purple to white.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite, oval leaves with prominent teeth along the edges. They feel rough and somewhat hairy to the touch, similar to nettle leaves but without the sting.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Square stems that feel distinctly four-angled when rolled between your fingers - a telltale sign of the mint family. Plants grow 1-3 feet tall with branching stems.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark nutlets develop after flowering, tucked inside the persistent flower cups. These dry fruits often rattle when the plant is shaken in late summer.

habitat: Look for bifid hemp-nettle in disturbed areas like roadsides, waste places, gardens, and field edges throughout New England. It thrives in rich, moist soils and often appears where the ground has been recently disturbed. You'll commonly find it mixed with other weedy plants in areas with partial shade to full sun.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with their characteristic square stems becoming apparent as they grow taller through late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from mid to late summer when the distinctive split-lipped flowers are most visible and useful for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed heads develop, with the square stems and opposite leaf arrangement still visible until frost kills the annual plants.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: The genus name Galeopsis literally means 'weasel-like' because early botanists thought the hooded upper lip of the flower looked like a sneaky weasel's face peering out at them!
confusionNotes: Often mistaken for wild mint species, but bifid hemp-nettle lacks the distinctive minty smell when crushed. It can also be confused with other members of the mint family, but the large, distinctly split-lipped flowers are unique. Memory trick: 'Bifid' sounds like 'divided' - look for that split lower lip!
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, this plant is completely unrelated to true hemp (Cannabis) or stinging nettles (Urtica). The 'hemp-nettle' name is purely based on superficial leaf resemblance and causes unnecessary confusion for new plant learners.
compareHints: Bifid hemp-nettle differs from its close relative common hemp-nettle mainly in flower size and lip structure - bifid has larger flowers with more prominently split lower lips. Both share the square stems and opposite leaves of the mint family, but bifid hemp-nettle's flowers are generally showier and more distinctly two-toned in coloration.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common hemp-nettle differs from its relative bifid hemp-nettle primarily in flower structure and leaf details, though bifid hemp-nettle is much less common in New England.
